title: On Trial Until It Proves Itself: A Boot Counter, Rollback by Itself, and Why Confirming at Start-Up Is the Same as Not Checking

questions.question: Why is the try used up before the release runs?
options: A release too broken to say anything must still cost a try: a counter changed only by a working release does not count crashes
questions.explanation: The counter lives in the boot loader.

questions.question: A release hangs: up, never healthy, never crashing. What rolls it back?
options: A supervisor that resets the robot at the health deadline: without one it is up for ever doing nothing

questions.question: A release is healthy at 20 s and crashes at 40 s. It confirms itself when the program starts. What happens?
options: Confirmed at second zero, then crashes with nothing to roll back to: a crash loop, 20 boots and not up
questions.explanation: Confirming early makes the trial a decoration.

questions.question: With a crash at 120 s and a healthy time of 20 s, which soaks catch it?
options: 100 s and longer: 20 plus the soak must come after the crash, so 90 s is not enough

questions.question: What can the code not know about the soak?
options: How long it takes the failure to show: a leak, a filling disk or a daily task is found from what the robot does
questions.explanation: A number to be found, not to be chosen.

questions.question: Why is a health check not a safety check?
options: A release can be healthy by its own checks and dangerous: the first drive of a new release is with the wheels off the ground
questions.explanation: Lesson 19-10 is about the other kind of failure.
